title: Introduction to Social Networking
summary: Social networking is linking and networking with friends and family on the web. Sites let members create profiles, add members to their network, share information, photographs and videos, organize events, chat and play games. Popular ones: Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, LinkedIn, WhatsApp, YouTube and blogs.

Advantages: connectivity (people worldwide share thoughts and ideas); real-time updates and responses, with the option to forward updates; education (students learn from experts at any time and place); marketing and growth (promote a business and take online orders); awareness (people of one profession such as farmers learn new techniques; donations for noble causes such as the Kerala floods of August 2018).

Disadvantages: hacking (profiles need only an e-mail id or mobile number, so fake identity is possible; stealing someone's identity is called hacking); risk of frauds (fraudulent links and requests for personal information); cyber or online bullying (can cause depression or suicidal tendencies); addiction (and health issues from long use of laptop or mobile).

LinkedIn (www.linkedin.com) is a business and employment-oriented networking platform that focuses on our professional journey: a well-written professional profile and job search. Steps: enter your details to create an account; sign in; update academic and other details in the edit profile section; use the Jobs section to see recommended jobs or search manually; right-click the Me tab, choose Settings and Privacy to secure the account and change Login and security. Searching a job: enter a keyword (job title, location or company) in the Search bar, select a suggestion or click the Search icon; tabs on the results page: All, People, Jobs, Content, Companies, Groups, Schools; use All Filters (Sort by, Date posted, Companies) and click Apply; LinkedIn Learning gives videos. Writing an article: visit Home, click Write an article, add a header image, add the headline and post body, create the footer, then Publish and share.

Facebook (www.facebook.com), created by Mark Zuckerberg, lets users make profiles, upload photos and videos, send messages and stay connected; it can promote an institution and tag friends. Secure the account: click the down arrow, Settings, Security and Login; enable Two-factor authentication; use privacy settings so that only friends see your details; Manage Blocking blocks apps and unwanted users. Add a friend: click the search bar, type the name, select from the list, click Add Friend; the person must accept the request. Share: Create Post at the top of the home page; add text, photo/video, feeling or tag friends; select the audience – Public, Friends, Friends except, Specific friends or Only me – and click Post.

Twitter (www.twitter.com) is a free microblogging service where registered members broadcast short posts called tweets (maximum 280 characters) and follow other users. It is a public platform: anyone can follow anyone in one click (unlike Facebook or LinkedIn where connections are approved). A hashtag (#keyword) connects a tweet to a topic. To tweet type the message in the 'What's happening' box and click Tweet (photos, GIF or video can be included). To follow someone search for the account and select it.

A blog (weblog) is a website like a diary or journal; the person who writes is a blogger and the process is blogging; a vlog is a video blog. Create a blog on www.blogger.com: click Create your blog, sign in with Gmail, click Create New Blog, enter the title, address and template, click New post, write and click Publish; the blog can then be edited or shared.

YouTube (www.youtube.com) is a Google video-sharing platform that can be used without an account; sign in with the Gmail account to save preferences; use the search box; Subscribe to a channel to get notifications of new videos; used for online lectures and training; one can create a channel and upload videos. Users must follow cyber ethics on all sites.

The information a user leaves behind on the internet (websites visited, e-mails sent, information submitted to online services) is the digital footprint. Passive digital footprint: data collected without the owner's knowledge (data exhaust). Active digital footprint: personal data deliberately released by the user to share information, e.g. on social media. To reduce the trail: check privacy settings, remove old accounts, unsubscribe from mailing lists, register with a different e-mail, use stealth (private) browsing, think before you post and use anti-tracking tools.
